dedupe_keys.name: 2025 m7 7 myanmar earthquake rapid building damage assessment from insar with a causal bayesian network designsafe prj 5897

description: This DesignSafe publication reports a rapid city-scale building damage assessment after the magnitude 7.7 earthquake that struck Myanmar's Sagaing Region near Mandalay on 28 March 2025, which the authors say killed about 5,350 people. Susu Xu (Stony Brook University), Xuechun Li (Johns Hopkins University), and Paula Bürgi and David Wald (USGS) used a variational causal Bayesian network that combines InSAR change detection at 30 m resolution with empirical landslide and liquefaction models and building footprints. The method estimates damage and ground failure over large areas, attributes each building's damage to shaking or ground failure, and classifies thousands of buildings into five damage states, from none to collapse, within days of the event; the authors validated it against high-resolution Maxar optical imagery. Coverage: the area affected by the March 2025 earthquake around Mandalay and Sagaing. Access: one report PDF of about 24 MB in the DesignSafe Data Depot, DOI 10.17603/ds2-d7xd-1869, published 16 April 2025, data type report. Licence: Creative Commons Attribution, as stated on the publication; free. Caveats: the publication is a report of maps and results, not a building-level data file, and accuracy figures are summarised in the report, not on the landing page. Simulation uses are rapid post-earthquake exposure and damage inputs for emergency response and a benchmark for remote-sensing damage models. Related records: the DesignSafe Data Depot, USGS PAGER and Türkiye 2023 damage-state mapping records.

name: 2025 M7.7 Myanmar earthquake: rapid building damage assessment from InSAR with a causal Bayesian network (DesignSafe PRJ-5897)
outcomes: Building-by-building damage in five classes (none, slight, moderate, partial collapse, collapse) was estimated within days of the 28 March 2025 earthquake and damage was attributed to shaking or ground failure; the results were validated against high-resolution Maxar imagery.
